name: Rafael Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, 58, a junior developer at a tech company that runs building-meter dashboards. My two-year college diploma got me into software, but I still need a senior review when an alert behaves oddly. I use AI now and then after a teammate shows me a sound test; a building manager's handwritten reset time once saved me from a wrong code fix. My partner sorts mail full-time, our children are grown, and we rent a flat with a spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our customers a building meter can send a bad reading without anyone using AI. I maintain the dashboard code at a tech company and check a week's numbers against the building manager's handwritten reset time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI only saves a little time, I think our household stays steady. I am still a junior developer after a two-year diploma, but my pay is typical, my partner sorts mail full-time, and we have five months of expenses saved; a few similar firms operate nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing meter-alert tickets and comparing readings with the reset log. We could add 70 to savings monthly while both wages hold, because our grown children now pay their own household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this picture. I want the fifth month in savings to stay there, but two current wages cover rent and ordinary spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the reset log change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A boiler reset at 6:10 made the dashboard show a sudden fall in use. My first code fix was wrong until the building manager showed me the handwritten reset time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your children help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children are grown and live away. They ring on Sundays, and none of their wages are part of our rent plan.

I'd keep **customer explanations** tied to actual readings.
think: I expect **two wages** to cover rent under modest AI change.
I have **five months saved** and a few nearby software employers.
do: Keep **fixing meter alerts** against the manager's reset log.
Save **70 monthly** while both wages hold and grown children pay their own bills.
feel: **Calm** about current income and a five-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could write much of our dashboard code and answer the easy customer tickets. I would ask whether the new alert catches a real meter fault rather than a boiler reset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior work could shrink, though I use AI now and then when a senior developer has shown me a good example. Five months saved helps, but at 58 I cannot assume another firm wants a learner at the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my lead for a paid afternoon to learn the AI fault-check method our senior tester already uses. If the lead agrees and it catches the known boiler-reset error without adding false alarms, I'd use it on one scheduled release; we'd postpone replacing our dining table until the team confirms its paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a repeatable test is worth learning. I am less keen on a tool that makes a tidy graph and then calls a reset a broken meter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the senior tester show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior tester compares a meter jump with the service log before marking it faulty. I want to reproduce the senior tester’s meter-and-service-log check with the old boiler case, not just learn where the AI button is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why defer the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our table wobbles but is safe. My partner and I can wait a year if the team's hours may change.

I'd say **junior dashboard work** could shrink as code gets cheaper.
think: I could lose **paid junior hours** even though I sometimes use AI.
I have **five months saved**, but no guaranteed replacement post.
do: Learn **senior tester's fault check** on paid time only if lead approves.
Use it on one **scheduled release** only if known reset is caught without false alarms.

feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to learn a proved check.

fieldNote: **Occasional AI use** fits his willingness to learn a proved method, not a blind rollout.
Lead approval, **paid time** and the known reset case gate one-release use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 might write our meter code before inspection robots arrive around 2031. I would want the firm to give us a dated decision about junior posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company could let junior developers go first. My partner's postal wage pays rent but not all our food and travel; five months saved gives us a search, not a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd check the two nearby software firms and the utility's meter-data desk for actual paid vacancies and shift hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only for a signed post whose wage with my partner's covers rent, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek available paid work outside software and use savings for bills while we contact the landlord before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my wage before an offer exists. The reserve buys months, not a promise from the utility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the boiler-reset correction without the customer's address. The useful part is how a service log changed a false alert, not how pretty the chart looked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do shift hours matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's mail shift starts before dawn, so I would check a new job's hours before accepting it. A role that made my partner miss paid shifts could leave us worse off even with my new wage.

say: I'd ask for **dated cut notice** if 2028 thinking AI replaces dashboard code.
I'd check **real utility vacancies** before naming a fallback.
think: I expect **junior developers** could be cut first.
I cannot cover **food and travel** on the postal wage alone.
do: Check **local firms** and utility for actual paid openings and hours now.

If none qualifies, seek **available paid work** using savings and contact landlord before arrears.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss despite five months saved.
S2.quote: The reserve buys months, not a promise from the utility.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches meter code before inspection robots around 2031.
A signed wage must cover **household bills** after any effect on his partner's postal shifts.

steps.text: Check two nearby firms and utility for paid openings and shift hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us find out whether the utility still pays someone to reconcile meter records. Thinking AI reaches the dashboard first, and inspection robots would follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be out of junior coding before 2031, so I will not spend five years waiting for a retirement date. I would move to a meter-data role only if there is a real paid vacancy and the work is something I can do after a proper handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the utility for its written meter-data job tasks, pay and shift pattern, then shadow the current clerk only if my manager approves paid time. If a vacancy opens and its signed wage with my partner's covers rent, food and travel without costing postal shifts, I'd apply; after 2031 I'd move only on that signed offer, otherwise keep my developer wage while it lasts and seek other paid local work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to see a full shift before changing jobs. I am not paying to train for a desk that has no opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to learn from the clerk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clerk has to match a meter number to a service visit before correcting a bill. I could learn that from a paid shadow shift, but I would not handle a customer's account without permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would compare the utility shift sheet with the postal roster. We would not trade a certain postal wage for a supposedly better job whose hours clash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2036 could take me near 68, but a long runway is not the same as a retirement income. Thinking AI reaches our code in 2036, and inspection robots could follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five months saved and two wages make today manageable. I have not checked any pension figure, and I do not know whether the rent on this larger flat will still make sense once we stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the meter fixes and save 70 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare them with rent and bills. If the verified income will not cover this flat, my partner and I would view a smaller accessible rental; after 2036 we'd move only if we both agree, a suitable place is actually offered, and the lower rent after deposit and moving costs leaves enough for food and travel, otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a distant change, but I can check actual figures before moving a box. I would not call a cheaper advert a cheaper home until the deposit and travel are included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a smaller flat work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The spare bedroom is mostly storage since our children moved out. A smaller place could work if the stairs are manageable, because my partner's knees ache after a mail shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children pay the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children can help carry boxes if they want, but I will not assume they can pay the deposit. That has to come from our own savings after the rent comparison.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the company could cut junior code work before a utility or software post is available. Dated notice, real written shifts and wages, and time to compare them with my partner's postal roster would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether our spare room is worth its rent. It may not be once we see the retirement figures, but I will not move my partner on the strength of an advert alone.

headlineQuote: I will not move my partner on the strength of an advert alone.
portrait: Rafael, **58**, is a junior building-meter developer with a two-year diploma who checks alerts against physical reset logs.
His **typical wage**, partner's full-time postal pay, five-month reserve and a few nearby software firms support today's rent.
He uses AI **occasionally**, learning a senior tester's method only on approved paid time and after a known error is caught.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** him; a utility role needs a real vacancy, signed household pay and hours compatible with postal shifts.
By 2036 he considers **smaller accessible housing** only after verified retirement figures, partner agreement, an actual offer and full cost comparison.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior code wage before a qualifying utility vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Dated cut notice**, written shifts and wages, and time to compare postal hours would help.
